articles.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
articles.summary: The prime minister is embarking on a UK tour with a series of announcements aimed at easing living costs.
articles.content:
Consumers will benefit from an end to so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices", Andy Burnham has said.

The prime minister is bringing forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, to make it easier to cancel subscriptions.

Burnham is also planning to outlaw shops using fake "was" prices, which he said trick shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers £400m a year in total, or up to £170 per person.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a £2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.
articles.reasoning: The article describes government actions to protect consumers from subscription traps and misleading pricing, which have a broad positive impact on the general public by easing the cost of living and improving consumer rights. The measures are substantive, with clear details on implementation and expected financial benefits for consumers.
articles.personality_title: UK government speeds up ban on subscription traps and fake prices to help families
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people in the UK are struggling with rising living costs. To help, the government is making changes to protect consumers from tricky subscription services and misleading shop prices.

**What happened** – Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that new rules to stop subscription traps and fake “was” prices in shops will start earlier than planned, by January 2027 instead of next spring. These rules make it easier for people to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stop shops from using fake discounts to trick buyers. The government will also ask the public for ideas on how to apply these rules in the fall.

**Impact** – These changes could save consumers about £400 million a year, or up to £170 per person. This means families can keep more money in their pockets. Consumer groups have praised the plan because it targets unfair business practices that hurt shoppers. It also shows the government’s effort to give people relief during tough financial times.

**What’s next step** – The government will hold a consultation this autumn to decide exactly how to enforce the new rules. Meanwhile, other cost-saving measures like cheaper bus fares and lower electricity taxes are already in place. More government plans will be revealed in the Budget on October 28.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UK government is acting faster to stop subscription traps and fake shop prices, aiming to save families money and make shopping fairer.

articles.title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
articles.summary: Parents should not have to buy more than three branded items, plus a tie for secondary schools.
articles.content:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.
articles.reasoning: The new law limiting the number of required branded school uniform items reduces financial burdens on families, making education more affordable and equitable. This policy has broad societal impact by supporting families across England and promoting fairness in school requirements.
articles.personality_title: New school uniform rules in England to help families save money
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Starting in September, a new law in England will limit how many branded school uniform items parents must buy for their children. This aims to reduce the cost of school uniforms.

**What happened** – The law says schools can require no more than three items with a school logo, like blazers or jumpers, plus a tie for secondary schools. About one-quarter of schools will need to adjust their uniform rules to follow this change. For example, Co-op Academy Belle Vue in Manchester is cutting its branded items from seven to just three plus a tie.

**Impact** – This change can save families up to £50 per child on uniform costs. At Co-op Academy Belle Vue, the average cost of branded uniform items dropped from about £102 last year to around £54 this year. These savings make it easier for families to afford school clothes and reduce pressure to buy many expensive branded items.

**What's next step** – Schools will update their uniform policies to meet the new rules by September. Some schools will also look for new suppliers to offer lower-cost uniforms. Over time, this could lead to more affordable and fair school uniform options across England.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The new uniform law limits branded items to three, helping families save money and making school uniforms more affordable in England.

articles.title: You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check
articles.summary: Some people need to ensure they are named on their energy bill before the deadline to qualify for help.
articles.content:
Millions of people will learn of the level of winter energy prices later this month, when Ofgem announces the quarterly price cap for the three months from October.

To help those who might struggle to pay, energy companies distribute the £150 Warm Home Discount to about six million households in the winter. Households in receipt of housing benefit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and universal credit qualify.

Households who are eligible should get the discount automatically, provided their supplier has over 1,000 customers.

However, that only happens if your name is on the bill and you are receiving one of these benefits. It can also help suppliers offer better support, such as repayment plans, to those who have energy debt.

Someone might not be named on their electricity bill if they have recently moved house.

Eligible customers on pre-payment meters who use a key or card to top up will also need to ensure that their household's account is registered in their name.

"If you know someone who might benefit, please start spreading the word and encourage them to check they are named on their energy bill," said Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

The government also said that 345,000 Scottish low-income households would now automatically receive the rebate in the winter, bringing Scotland's policy in line with England and Wales.

Previously, eligible Scottish households have had to apply for the scheme.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a government-backed financial support scheme (Warm Home Discount) that helps millions of low-income households reduce their energy bills during winter, which has a meaningful positive impact on vulnerable populations and promotes social equity. The expansion of automatic rebates in Scotland further broadens the benefit's reach, making it significant and substantive.
articles.personality_title: Millions can save £150 on winter energy bills with simple check
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every winter, energy prices rise, making it harder for many families to pay their bills. To help, the UK government offers a £150 Warm Home Discount to eligible low-income households.

**What happened** – This winter, about six million households will receive this discount automatically if they qualify and their name is on the energy bill. People who get certain benefits, like housing benefit or universal credit, are eligible. The government also made it easier for 345,000 low-income households in Scotland to get the discount automatically, without having to apply.

**Impact** – This support helps families afford their energy during cold months, reducing financial stress. Making the rebate automatic in Scotland closes a gap so more people get help without extra steps. Checking that your name is on the bill is important because otherwise, you might miss out on the discount even if you qualify.

**What's next step** – People should check their energy bills now to make sure their name is listed, especially if they recently moved or use a pre-payment meter. Sharing this information with friends and family can help more people benefit. Energy suppliers will continue to support customers with payment plans for those who owe money.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Millions of low-income households can save £150 on winter energy bills by ensuring their name is on the bill and qualifying for the Warm Home Discount.
